name: Technetium
blurb: Technetium has no stable isotope, yet 99mTc is the most used radionuclide in medicine, roughly 30 to 40 million scans a year eluted from a bench-top 99Mo/99mTc generator. It is invisible to MR; what matters in the magnet room is that a patient may arrive carrying it at picomolar chemical dose, which perturbs B0 by nothing measurable.
mrNotes: 99mTc is the 142.7 keV isomer of 99Tc, I = 1/2, half life 6.007 h, emitting a 140.5 keV gamma in 89% of decays. Its nuclear moment is not among the recommended tabulated values, so no gamma is quoted here.

The 99Tc ground state is a genuinely good NMR nucleus. Any technetium sample is necessarily 100% 99Tc, and at that enrichment its receptivity is 2200 times natural-abundance 13C, which is why 99Tc NMR is the standard tool for Tc speciation in nuclear waste chemistry.
Simultaneous SPECT/MR stayed rare because photomultiplier tubes fail inside B0; CdZnTe direct-conversion detectors, which do not, are the reason MR-compatible gamma cameras exist at all.
Pertechnetate is the shift reference but its 99Tc shift moves with temperature and counter-ion, so a 99Tc chemical shift quoted without those conditions is worth little.

Technetium has no stable isotope, so every bulk susceptibility is measured on synthesised metal and the number is governed by the purity of that sample. The +270e-6 cm3/mol carried by older element tables has not been traced to a source.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity is zero at natural abundance because there is no natural technetium; at the 100% enrichment of any real sample it is 0.375 relative to 1H and 2200 relative to 13C. 90.1 MHz at 9.4 T. The IUPAC Xi implies gamma/2pi = 9.5835 MHz/T, 0.13% above the value derived from the moment used here. That sign is not an error: Xi is the frequency of a shielded 99Tc nucleus in TcO4-, and for a d0 transition-metal oxoanion the absolute shielding is expected to be negative, the paramagnetic term outweighing the free-atom diamagnetic one, so about -1290 ppm is an ordinary value rather than an impossible one. The 90.1 MHz quoted above follows the measured ratio; the moment-derived gamma would give 90.0 MHz.
99mTc, the 142.7 keV metastable state. Detected by gamma camera, never by NMR: it is gone in hours and its magnetic moment is not reliably tabulated, so mu and gamma are left null.
isotopes.label: 99mTc

name: Ruthenium
blurb: Ruthenium supplies two of the least tractable NMR nuclei in the periodic table, 99Ru and 101Ru, both near 2 MHz/T and both quadrupolar. Its only routine appearance in an MR department is as a 106Ru episcleral plaque on the globe of a patient being scanned for uveal melanoma.
mrNotes: 99Ru is the observe isotope despite its lower gamma and abundance, because 101Ru carries Q = 46 fm2 against 7.9 fm2 and so broadens about 34 times faster in the same electric field gradient.
At 9.4 T, 99Ru sits at 18.4 MHz. Solid-state 99Ru NMR of diamagnetic ruthenium compounds was first demonstrated in 2004 and still needs high field and hours of averaging.
The 99Ru shift range exceeds 18000 ppm from [Ru(CN)6]4-, among the widest of any nucleus, so the shift is very informative once you can detect the line.
106Ru (373.6 d) beta plaques for uveal melanoma are silver-encapsulated and non-ferromagnetic, but they are still a centimetre of metal on the orbit and will void a gradient-echo scan.

isotopes.notes: 1.9 times more receptive than 99Ru, but Q = 46 fm2 makes the line about 34 times broader for the same electric field gradient, so 99Ru is the isotope people actually use.

Receptivity 0.85 relative to natural-abundance 13C, 18.4 MHz at 9.4 T. The small quadrupole moment, 7.9 fm2, is what makes 99Ru usable at all. The Stone moment used here agrees with the IUPAC Xi to 40 ppm, so it is effectively the uncorrected NMR value rather than a shielding-corrected one.

name: Rhodium
blurb: 103Rh is spin 1/2 at 100% natural abundance with gamma/2pi = -1.346 MHz/T, the smallest of any spin-1/2 nucleus; its receptivity is about one fifth that of natural-abundance 13C. The compensation is T1 of minutes, which is why 103Rh is now being pursued as a very long-lived hyperpolarized label.
mrNotes: IUPAC fixes the 103Rh shift scale by an arbitrary frequency, Xi = 3.16 MHz exactly, because no single rhodium compound could be agreed as a reference.

1H to 103Rh polarization transfer in Rh(acac)3 and in rhodium formate paddlewheel complexes gives large 103Rh enhancements with T1 of minutes, the basis of proposals for hyperpolarized markers that survive far longer than 13C.
Rhodium is also the metal in the classic PHIP hydrogenation catalysts such as [Rh(dppb)(COD)]BF4, used to make hyperpolarized hydroxyethyl propionate for angiography.
At 3 T, 103Rh resonates at 3.9 MHz, below the tuning range of clinical broadband hardware.

isotopes.notes: Lowest gamma of any spin-1/2 nucleus; receptivity 0.186 relative to natural-abundance 13C even at 100% abundance. T1 of minutes means indirect detection through 31P or 1H is the normal route to a 103Rh shift.

name: Palladium
blurb: 105Pd is the only NMR-active palladium isotope and a hard one: 22% abundance, gamma/2pi = -1.945 MHz/T and Q = +66 fm2, so lines appear only in near-cubic sites such as [PdCl6]2-. Palladium's real presence around a scanner is 103Pd brachytherapy seeds and an unusually large paramagnetic susceptibility.
mrNotes: Palladium metal has molar susceptibility +540e-6 cm3/mol, a volume susceptibility of about +767 ppm in SI terms against -9.7 ppm for copper and -9.0 ppm for soft tissue, so a palladium part near isocentre distorts B0 far more than its size suggests. Palladium is the classic strongly enhanced Pauli paramagnet and its susceptibility peaks near 85 K, so the figure is a room-temperature one good to a few percent.

103Pd (17.0 d, electron capture, 21 keV X-rays) is the low-energy alternative to 125I for permanent prostate brachytherapy. The seeds are titanium-clad and non-ferromagnetic but still leave a signal void on gradient echo.

EasySpin and Stone give mu(105Pd) = -0.638 muN, hence gamma/2pi = -1.9453 MHz/T; older NMR tables quote -1.957 MHz/T from mu = -0.642 muN. The 0.6% spread is larger than any shielding correction and reflects real disagreement in the measurement.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity 1.5 relative to natural-abundance 13C, and Q = 66 fm2 restricts observation to octahedral or tetrahedral sites. Essentially no solution 105Pd work is done outside hexahalopalladates.

name: Silver
blurb: 107Ag and 109Ag are spin 1/2 at close to 50:50 abundance and, after 103Rh, the least sensitive spin-1/2 nuclei there are, with T1 of hundreds of seconds. Silver's day job in MR is hardware: plating on RF conductors, and the Ag/AgCl in every MR-compatible ECG electrode.
mrNotes: 109Ag is the preferred observe isotope, gamma/2pi = -1.990 against -1.731 MHz/T, worth a factor of 1.4 in receptivity even though it is slightly less abundant.

Silver has the lowest bulk resistivity of any metal, 1.59 microohm cm at 20 C, so silver-plating a copper conductor lowers RF surface resistance and raises unloaded Q. The gain only shows up in small coils that are not sample-noise dominated.
109Ag T1 can exceed 500 s in diamagnetic solids and solutions, so a relaxation agent such as Cr(acac)3 or a recycle delay of tens of minutes is standard practice.

Silver is diamagnetic, volume susceptibility about -24 ppm in SI against -9 ppm for soft tissue, so an Ag/AgCl electrode shifts local B0 by a few ppm rather than the hundreds of ppm a ferromagnetic snap would.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity 0.20 relative to natural-abundance 13C, and only 16.2 MHz at 9.4 T, low enough that probe and preamplifier design rather than the sample set the noise figure.

Receptivity 0.29 relative to natural-abundance 13C, the better of the two. Silver shifts are very solvent and counter-ion sensitive, which is why AgNO3 in D2O rather than solid AgNO3 is the reference.

name: Cadmium
blurb: 111Cd and 113Cd are spin 1/2 with gamma near -9.07 and -9.49 MHz/T, close to 13C, and about 12% abundant each, which makes 113Cd genuinely usable. Its classic role is as a spectroscopic stand-in for NMR-silent Zn(II) and Ca(II) in proteins; its modern one is as the Cd in the CdZnTe detectors that let gamma cameras work inside a magnet.
mrNotes: 113Cd has receptivity 7.9 times natural-abundance 13C and 111Cd 7.3, so either is a comfortable direct-detect nucleus on a standard broadband probe.
Cd-S coordination in metallothionein and zinc fingers resonates near +600 to +750 ppm and Cd-O sites near 0 to +100 ppm, so the 113Cd shift reads out the donor-atom set directly.

CdZnTe, roughly Cd0.9Zn0.1Te, is the room-temperature direct-conversion detector in modern SPECT cameras and in MR-compatible PET inserts, replacing the photomultiplier tube that cannot operate in B0.

111Cd is the daughter of 111In and the standard probe nucleus for perturbed angular correlation spectroscopy, a different way of reading the same electric field gradient an NMR quadrupole coupling reports.

isotopes.notes: Chosen over 113Cd when the sample is 111Cd enriched for perturbed angular correlation work or when a 113Cd spinning sideband overlaps. 26.1 MHz at 2.89 T.
The standard cadmium nucleus. Dimethylcadmium is the IUPAC primary reference but is pyrophoric, so 0.1 M Cd(ClO4)2 in D2O is the usual working secondary standard.

name: Indium
blurb: 115In is 95.7% abundant with I = 9/2 and a paper receptivity near 2000 times 13C, but Q = +77 fm2 means that outside a cubic site the line is megahertz wide. Clinically, indium means 111In: OctreoScan, labelled leukocytes and DTPA cisternography.
mrNotes: 111In (2.80 d, 171 and 245 keV gammas) carries 111In-pentetreotide, 111In-oxine labelled white cells for occult infection and intrathecal 111In-DTPA for CSF leak studies. None of it is MR visible.
115In and 113In differ by only 0.2% in gamma, so they are never resolved as separate species; 115In is used for its 22-fold abundance advantage.
Indium metal is the standard cold gasket for cryostat and NMR probe seals: ductile to 4 K, melting at 156.6 C, diamagnetic, and superconducting below 3.41 K.
113mIn (99.5 min) from a 113Sn/113mIn generator was an early short-lived imaging agent and is now essentially historical.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity 1980 times natural-abundance 13C, one of the highest of any quadrupolar nucleus, but only cubic or near-cubic environments give a line you can find. 115In is itself radioactive, beta- with a 4.4e14 y half life, which is why it is treated as stable.
Receptivity 88 times 13C. Used only when 115In is unavailable or when the isotope shift is the point.

The workhorse indium SPECT nuclide. mu = +5.503 muN is well determined, so gamma is quoted; the quadrupole moment is not tabulated on the 2018 recommended scale, which revised the indium Q values down by about 10%, so q is left null.

name: Tin
blurb: Tin is in the magnet long before it is in the patient: Nb3Sn, Tc = 18.3 K, is the conductor that carries persistent current in every NMR magnet above roughly 18 T, where NbTi has run out of upper critical field. Among the nuclei, 119Sn is a well behaved spin 1/2 probe with a shift range of thousands of ppm.
mrNotes: Nb3Sn is brittle and must be wound and then reacted near 650 C, which is a large part of why 1 GHz class NMR magnets cost what they do; NbTi alone covers everything up to about 18 T.
119Sn is the observe nucleus: gamma/2pi = -15.94 MHz/T and 8.59% abundance give receptivity 26.5 times natural-abundance 13C, against 20.7 for 117Sn.
117mSn (13.8 d) emits conversion electrons with a sub-millimetre range and is used as 117mSn-DTPA for bone pain palliation, with markedly less marrow toxicity than 89Sr or 153Sm.
Dental amalgam is a silver-tin-mercury alloy. It is not ferromagnetic, but it is metallic and it is the usual cause of the signal void that ruins oral cavity and temporomandibular joint imaging.

The -37.4e-6 cm3/mol is gray (alpha) tin, the diamond-structure semiconductor stable below 13.2 C, and it is the only tin the source tabulates. The tin an imaging department meets is white (beta) tin, in solder, in dental amalgam and in Nb3Sn, which is an ordinary metal and weakly paramagnetic; neither the magnitude nor the sign of this cell applies to it.

isotopes.notes: The standard tin nucleus, 45.9 MHz at 2.89 T. Large negative NOE from 1H means inverse-gated decoupling or a DEPT-type transfer is normal practice.
Almost as good as 119Sn and only 4.4% lower in gamma; useful when a 119Sn resonance is obscured or when 117Sn-119Sn coupling is being measured.

Only 0.34% abundant, receptivity 0.71 relative to 13C, so it is used almost only for isotope effect studies. The EasySpin moment is given to four figures and is about 400 ppm off the value implied by the IUPAC Xi.

name: Antimony
blurb: Both antimony isotopes are quadrupolar with large moments, 121Sb at -54.3 fm2 and 123Sb at -69.2 fm2, so lines appear only in near-octahedral sites such as [SbCl6]- and [Sb(OH)6]-. Antimony has no role in magnetic resonance beyond materials work.
mrNotes: 121Sb has the better combination, I = 5/2 at 57.2% abundance with receptivity 546 times natural-abundance 13C, but any distortion from octahedral symmetry broadens the line past usefulness.
Sb2Te3 thermoelectrics and topological insulators are where most 121Sb and 123Sb solid-state NMR is actually done.
125Sb (2.76 y) is a fission product found alongside 99Tc in legacy nuclear waste; it has no imaging use.

isotopes.notes: 29.5 MHz at 2.89 T and 95.8 MHz at 9.4 T. Receptivity 546 relative to natural-abundance 13C on paper.

Lower gamma but higher spin. Q is 27% larger than 121Sb, yet the quadrupolar relaxation spin factor (2I+3)/(I^2(2I-1)) is 2.35 times smaller at I = 7/2, so 123Sb lines are about 30% narrower than 121Sb lines in the same site.

name: Tellurium
blurb: 125Te is spin 1/2 at 7.07% abundance with receptivity 13 times natural-abundance 13C and a shift range of nearly 5000 ppm, which makes it an exquisitely sensitive reporter of coordination. Tellurium reaches the MR suite as the Te in CdZnTe detectors and as the stable daughter of every 125I brachytherapy seed.
mrNotes: 125Te shifts run from about -4100 ppm for six-coordinate tellurium to roughly +1000 ppm for two-coordinate organotellurides relative to dimethyl telluride, so referencing and temperature control matter more than for most spin 1/2 nuclei.
123Te is nominally radioactive by electron capture with a half life above 9e16 y, which is why it is handled as stable. At 0.89% abundance it is almost never the isotope of choice.
125I decays to stable 125Te, so a permanent prostate seed ends its life as a few micrograms of tellurium inside titanium.
CdZnTe is the room-temperature direct-conversion detector in modern SPECT cameras and MR-compatible PET inserts.

isotopes.notes: 38.9 MHz at 2.89 T. Dimethyl telluride is the IUPAC reference but is foul smelling and air sensitive, so diphenyl ditelluride at +422 ppm is a common working secondary standard.
Receptivity 0.96 relative to natural-abundance 13C, essentially the same sensitivity as 13C but with none of its ubiquity. Used mainly for 123Te-125Te isotope shift work.

name: Iodine
blurb: Iodine is the contrast element of the other modality: 300 to 370 mg I/mL of iodinated agent for CT, cleared by the same glomerular route as gadolinium chelates. 127I itself is 100% abundant with I = 5/2, but Q = -69.6 fm2 makes it observable only in near-spherical sites, and it has never been imaged in vivo.
mrNotes: 127I quadrupole coupling constants reach 214 MHz in low-symmetry solids, so only iodide in cubic salts and symmetric oxoanions such as periodate give lines narrow enough to detect. Covalent iodine is effectively invisible.

123I (13.2 h, 159 keV) is the SPECT thyroid and ioflupane nuclide, 131I (8.02 d, beta plus a 364 keV gamma) the therapy nuclide, 124I (4.18 d) the PET dosimetry surrogate and 125I (59.4 d) the permanent brachytherapy seed.

Iodinated CT contrast is diamagnetic and MR silent, so it does not compromise a subsequent MR scan; it does share a renal clearance pathway with gadolinium chelates, which matters when both are given in one day.

The 2018 recommended quadrupole moment for 127I, -69.6 fm2, replaced the older -78.9 fm2, so electric field gradients derived from a measured coupling constant using the old moment come out about 13% too small.

isotopes.notes: Receptivity 558 times natural-abundance 13C on paper, 24.7 MHz at 2.89 T, and almost never usable because of quadrupolar broadening. No meaningful shift range is tabulated, so shiftRange is left null.
SPECT thyroid uptake and 123I-ioflupane (DaTscan) for dopamine transporter imaging. mu = +2.818 muN is well determined; Q has never been measured on the current scale, so q is null.
Positron emitter used for thyroid cancer PET dosimetry and for long-lived antibody labelling; its large gamma cascade makes quantification awkward. Moment not reliably tabulated, left null.
Permanent prostate brachytherapy seeds and radioimmunoassay. Decays by electron capture to stable 125Te. Q is tabulated only on the pre-2018 scale, so q is left null.
The long-lived fission product tracked in environmental and waste chemistry. Q here is on the 2018 recommended scale, the same scale as the 127I value.
Thyroid ablation and hyperthyroidism therapy; the 364 keV gamma allows post-therapy imaging. Q is tabulated only on the pre-2018 scale, so q is left null.

name: Xenon
blurb: 129Xe is why this column matters. Spin 1/2, 26.44% natural abundance, polarized to tens of percent by spin exchange with optically pumped rubidium vapour, and FDA approved since December 2022 for ventilation MRI of the lungs. Its 200 ppm dissolved-phase shifts let one breath report separately on airspace, interstitium and red blood cells.
mrNotes: On the biomedical scale with Xe gas at 0 ppm, dissolved 129Xe appears near 197 ppm in the alveolar membrane and interstitium and near 218 ppm in red blood cells; the RBC to membrane ratio is the standard readout for interstitial lung disease and pulmonary vascular disease.
In brain the peaks are gray matter 196 ppm, white matter 192 ppm, plasma and CSF near 200 ppm and red blood cells 217 ppm, all from a single breath hold at 1.5 T or 3 T.
Gas-phase 129Xe sits at 17.66 MHz where 1H is 63.87 MHz and at 34.09 MHz where 1H is 123.2 MHz, so every 129Xe study needs its own coil, transmit chain and usually its own preamplifier.

Gas T1 in the lung is roughly 20 s, set by paramagnetic O2, and dissolved-phase T1 in blood is a few seconds. The magnetization is not renewable, so every excitation permanently spends signal and flip angles are chosen accordingly.

isotopes.reference: XeOF4; Xe gas = 0 ppm in biomedical work
isotopes.notes: gamma here is derived from the Stone moment and is the shielding-free value. The working NMR value referenced to xenon gas is 11.777 MHz/T, 0.7% lower, because the xenon atom's own diamagnetic shielding is close to 6900 ppm; the IUPAC reference XeOF4 lies 5331 ppm to high frequency of the gas. Imaging gas is normally enriched to 83 to 87% 129Xe, worth a factor of about 3.2 in signal.

isotopes.reference: XeOF4; Xe gas = 0 ppm in biomedical work
isotopes.notes: Q = -11.4 fm2 means hyperpolarized 131Xe relaxes on wall and tissue contact through quadrupolar coupling, which makes it a surface probe but keeps its polarization and T1 far below 129Xe. 131Xe is the co-magnetometer partner to 129Xe in spin-based tests of fundamental physics. 10.1 MHz at 2.89 T.

81 keV gamma; the classic lung ventilation and cerebral blood flow agent for scintigraphy, now largely displaced by 99mTc-Technegas and by hyperpolarized 129Xe MRI. Not an NMR nucleus. Q is tabulated only on the pre-2018 scale and is left null.
